sources.quote: 1969 – Utah Girls Village

name: Utah Youth Village

sources.quote: Later, in 1988 our name was changed to Utah Youth Village because we started to serve as many boys as girls.
In 1969, there were no programs for struggling girls in Utah.

note: Second pass. The organisation began in 1969 as Utah Girls Village and took the Utah Youth Village name in 1988 (one search snippet said end of 1989); start is the year of the name.

name: Vanalden RTC

sources.quote: "FACILITYNAME":"EVOLVE TREATMENT VANALDEN","FACILITYNUMBER":"198209708","FACILITYTYPE":"GROUP HOME","LICENSEFIRSTDATE":"12/19/2019"
Since 2014, we've helped children and teens battling depression, anxiety, trauma and other emotional behavioral issues through multiple behavioral inpatient and outpatient rehab programs.

note: Second pass. California Community Care Licensing first licensed Evolve Treatment Vanalden (licensee Evolve Growth Initiatives LLC) on 19 Dec 2019, and it is still licensed. Evolve itself dates from 2014, so the house may have run earlier under another licence.

name: Vantage Point

sources.quote: Started by physics_gal, August 28, 2010, 04:56:38 PM
Vantage Point, (neurologically diverse adolescents ages 13-17).

note: Vantage Point by Aspiro (Aspiro Group, Provo/Mt. Pleasant UT) for neurodiverse teens; a Fornits thread shows it existed by August 2010 and Woodbury Reports lists it in December 2011. No opening or rename year found; vantagepointaspiro.com no longer resolves.

name: Vermont State Board of Education

sources.quote: In 1856 a law was passed providing for a board of education, chosen annually by the legislature.

note: Second pass. The 1900 US Bureau of Education history of education in Vermont dates the state board of education to an 1856 law. The board has been reorganised since then, so treat 1856 as when the body began.

name: VisionQuest

sources.quote: VisionQuest National, Ltd., was established in 1973 in Tucson, Arizona by founder Robert L. Burton.

note: 1973 is the company's founding; the company still runs programs in five states. The Hesperia, CA site lost its San Bernardino County contract after misconduct findings reported in 2007 (settled 2009), but no closing year for that site was found.

name: Vista Treatment Centers

sources.quote: The plaintiffs, who are now adults, were residents at Vista's facilities between 2003 and 2019.
In 2022 the center was reported to be about to close

note: Second pass. No founding date found; residents were there by 2003 (lower bound). The Salt Lake Tribune reported the closure in July 2022 after a 26-plaintiff lawsuit.

name: Vivant Behavioral Healthcare

sources.quote: Most of the former Sequel treatment centers that remain open are now controlled by Vivant Behavioral Healthcare, which was founded in 2021 by Jay Ripley, one of three people who founded Sequel in 1999.
In September 2021, Ripley formed Vivant Behavioral Healthcare to "buy a majority of the business of Sequel Youth & Family Services."

note: Formed September 2021 to buy most of Sequel's centres; its website (vivantbh.com, Prescott Valley AZ) is still up.

name: Waco Center for Youth

sources.quote: The Waco State Home, three miles northwest of the business section of Waco, was established as the State Home for Dependent and Neglected Children by the Thirty-sixth Legislature in 1919.
In 1979 the Texas Youth Commission transferred control of the Waco State Home to the Texas Department of Mental Health and Mental Retardation.

note: Founded 1919 as the State Home for Dependent and Neglected Children (Waco State Home); became Waco Center for Youth after the 1979 transfer to Texas MHMR.
